title: Your Life Touches More Lives Than You Know
author: Kathleen Schafer
summary: Kathleen Schafer argues that daily life feels inconsequential to many people, yet what we do matters far more than we realize because no one makes it through life alone. She starts from human interdependence and says independence and interdependence are not opposites, so a person can own their choices while recognizing how much others shape their life. She then narrows the lens to the ordinary people we touch in a day, from a spouse to a stranger in traffic, and asks what happens in them because of the quality of our presence. The point is awareness rather than guilt, since recognizing our influence is the first way to regain power. Leadership, in her framing, lives in the accumulated effect of how we move through the world and not only in rooms where big decisions are made. She closes with a small weekend experiment of full attention, patience, sincere thanks and unspoken compliments, along with three reflection questions.
points: Interdependence and personal responsibility coexist, and forgetting our dependence on others makes it easier to ignore the structures and people behind our own lives.
The quality of our presence changes how people leave an interaction, whether more seen and capable or more depleted.
Most of the ripples from our encouragement, our truths and even our tolerated behavior are never visible to us, but they exist.
Leadership begins in the accumulated effect of ordinary encounters and not only in consequential decisions.
The practical step is a small experiment: give full attention, say the compliment you usually only think, and thank people as if you mean it.
quotes: We can be fully responsible for our lives while recognizing that the quality of those lives is profoundly affected by one another.
We are an extraordinarily interconnected species, even though we sometimes like to imagine otherwise.
Do people generally leave an interaction with you a little more uplifted or a little more depleted? More seen or less seen? More capable, more hopeful, more themselves—or slightly diminished?
Because the first way we regain our power is by recognizing that we have it.

Most of us will never know the full reach of our lives. We will not see every ripple created by the encouragement we offered, the truth we spoke, the kindness we extended, the behavior we normalized, the thing we tolerated, or the moment when we chose not to act.
Not only in the rooms where consequential decisions are made, but in the accumulated effect of how we move through the world and what our presence makes possible for other people.
Give the person in front of you your full attention. Offer the compliment you usually only think. Be a little more patient. Ask the additional question.
